claim: ATF6α is a type-II transmembrane protein localized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: Activating transcription factor six alpha (ATF6α) is a type-II transmembrane protein localized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) where, with its close homolog ATF6β, it functions as an ER stress sensor in one of the three principal branches of the unfolded protein response (UPR) (Haze et al., 1999; Gardner et al., 2013).
evidence: The statement is directly supported by citations to prior work (Haze et al., 1999; Gardner et al., 2013).

claim: ATF6α functions as an ER stress sensor in one of the three principal branches of the unfolded protein response (UPR).
source: Activating transcription factor six alpha (ATF6α) is a type-II transmembrane protein localized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) where, with its close homolog ATF6β, it functions as an ER stress sensor in one of the three principal branches of the unfolded protein response (UPR) (Haze et al., 1999; Gardner et al., 2013).
evidence: The statement is directly supported by citations to prior work (Haze et al., 1999; Gardner et al., 2013).

claim: ATF6α target genes are exclusively cytoprotective, functioning to increase the folding capacity of the ER and restore ER homeostasis.
source: ATF6α target genes are exclusively cytoprotective, functioning to increase the folding capacity of the ER and restore ER homeostasis (Adachi et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2007).
evidence: The statement is directly supported by citations to prior work (Adachi et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2007).

claim: Cells or animals lacking ATF6α show impaired survival upon ER stress.
source: Cells or animals lacking ATF6α show impaired survival upon ER stress (Wu et al., 2007; Yamamoto et al., 2007).
evidence: The statement is directly supported by citations to prior work (Wu et al., 2007; Yamamoto et al., 2007).

claim: When demand exceeds the folding capacity of the ER, ATF6α is transported from the ER to the Golgi apparatus.
source: When demand exceeds the folding capacity of the ER, ATF6α is transported from the ER to the Golgi apparatus, where sequential cleavage by two Golgi-resident proteases – site-1 and site-2 proteases (S1P and S2P), respectively - releases its N-terminal domain (ATF6α-N) from the membrane as a functional b-Zip transcription factor.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: Sequential cleavage of ATF6α by site-1 and site-2 proteases (S1P and S2P) in the Golgi apparatus releases its N-terminal domain (ATF6α-N) from the membrane as a functional b-Zip transcription factor.
source: When demand exceeds the folding capacity of the ER, ATF6α is transported from the ER to the Golgi apparatus, where sequential cleavage by two Golgi-resident proteases – site-1 and site-2 proteases (S1P and S2P), respectively - releases its N-terminal domain (ATF6α-N) from the membrane as a functional b-Zip transcription factor.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: ATF6α-N is imported into the nucleus where it activates transcription of its target genes.
source: ATF6α-N is then imported into the nucleus (nuclear translocation) where it activates transcription of its target genes (Ye et al., 2000).
evidence: The statement is directly supported by a citation to prior work (Ye et al., 2000).

claim: The mechanism that retains ATF6α in the ER and then releases it to allow transport to the Golgi apparatus is unknown.
source: The mechanism that retains ATF6α in the ER and then releases it to allow transport to the Golgi apparatus is unknown.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: The mechanism whereby ATF6α senses ER stress has remained a mystery since its discovery in 1998.
source: The mechanism whereby ATF6α senses ER stress has remained a mystery since its discovery in 1998 (Yoshida et al., 1998).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by a citation (Yoshida et al., 1998).

claim: The lumenal domain of ATF6α (ATF6α-LD) dictates whether ATF6α localizes to the ER or to the Golgi apparatus.
source: The lumenal domain of ATF6α (ATF6α-LD) dictates whether ATF6α localizes to the ER or to the Golgi apparatus (Chen et al., 2002; Schindler and Schekman, 2009).
evidence: The statement is directly supported by citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2002; Schindler and Schekman, 2009).

claim: The soluble ATF6α-LD alone is sufficient to sense ER stress.
source: In fact, the soluble ATF6α-LD alone is sufficient to sense ER stress (Sato et al., 2011), and attaching the ATF6α-LD to the constitutively transported SNARE protein Sec22 is sufficient to retain Sec22 in the ER of unstressed cells, allowing its trafficking to the Golgi apparatus only upon ER stress (Schindler and Schekman, 2009).
evidence: The statement is directly supported by a citation to prior work (Sato et al., 2011).

claim: Attaching the ATF6α-LD to the constitutively transported SNARE protein Sec22 is sufficient to retain Sec22 in the ER of unstressed cells, allowing its trafficking to the Golgi apparatus only upon ER stress.
source: In fact, the soluble ATF6α-LD alone is sufficient to sense ER stress (Sato et al., 2011), and attaching the ATF6α-LD to the constitutively transported SNARE protein Sec22 is sufficient to retain Sec22 in the ER of unstressed cells, allowing its trafficking to the Golgi apparatus only upon ER stress (Schindler and Schekman, 2009).
evidence: The statement is directly supported by a citation to prior work (Schindler and Schekman, 2009).

claim: ATF6α-LD is ATF6α's stress-sensor and regulates its trafficking.
source: Thus ATF6α-LD is ATF6α's stress-sensor and regulates its trafficking.
evidence: The statement is an inference drawn from the preceding evidence about ATF6α-LD function.

claim: It is unclear what aspect of the folding environment ATF6α-LD is sensing, or if ATF6α senses misfolded proteins directly.
source: It is unclear what aspect of the folding environment ATF6α-LD is sensing, or if ATF6α senses misfolded proteins directly.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: The molecular machinery required to move ATF6α from the ER to the Golgi apparatus, the COPII coat, is positioned on the cytosolic side of the ER membrane.
source: The molecular machinery required to move ATF6α from the ER to the Golgi apparatus, the COPII coat, is positioned on the cytosolic side of the ER membrane.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: Activation of ATF6α requires transmitting the signal from the ER lumen to the cytosol.
source: Activation of ATF6α therefore requires transmitting the signal from the ER lumen to the cytosol (Schindler and Schekman, 2009; Nadanaka et al., 2004).
evidence: The statement is directly supported by citations to prior work (Schindler and Schekman, 2009; Nadanaka et al., 2004).

claim: It is unknown whether ATF6α interacts with the COPII coat directly or requires a transmembrane adaptor or traffics by bulk-flow after release from a transport-incompetent state.
source: It is unknown whether ATF6α interacts with the COPII coat directly or requires a transmembrane adaptor or traffics by bulk-flow after release from a transport-incompetent state.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: SREBP has a trafficking mechanism involving binding of a retention factor, INSIG, to a transport factor, SCAP.
source: SREBP, the membrane bound transcription factor that responds to low cholesterol, has an elegant trafficking mechanism involving binding of a retention factor, INSIG, to a transport factor, SCAP (Brown and Goldstein, 2009).
evidence: The statement is directly supported by a citation to prior work (Brown and Goldstein, 2009).

claim: SCAP, not SREBP, binds to and senses cholesterol and this binding regulates the interaction of SCAP both with its retention factor INSIG and with the COPII coat.
source: Indeed it is SCAP, not SREBP, that binds to and senses cholesterol and this binding regulates the interaction of SCAP both with its retention factor INSIG and with the COPII coat (Sun et al., 2007; Motamed et al., 2011).
evidence: The statement is directly supported by citations to prior work (Sun et al., 2007; Motamed et al., 2011).

claim: SREBP itself neither senses the signal nor interacts with the trafficking machinery.
source: SREBP itself neither senses the signal nor interacts with the trafficking machinery.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: A putative ACAP (ATF6α cleavage activating protein) and/or a putative INSIG-like ATF6α retention factor may remain to be discovered.
source: Similarly, a putative ACAP (ATF6α cleavage activating protein) and/or a putative INSIG-like ATF6α retention factor may remain to be discovered.
evidence: The statement is speculative, suggesting potential undiscovered factors.

claim: Ceapins are a class of pyrazole amides that inhibit selectively the processing of ATF6α by S1P and S2P in response to ER stress.
source: In the accompanying paper, we describe the identification of Ceapins, a class of pyrazole amides that inhibit selectively the processing of ATF6α by S1P and S2P in response to ER stress but not the other UPR sensors, including – surprisingly – ATF6β, or SREBP.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: Ceapins do not inhibit the other UPR sensors, including ATF6β or SREBP.
source: In the accompanying paper, we describe the identification of Ceapins, a class of pyrazole amides that inhibit selectively the processing of ATF6α by S1P and S2P in response to ER stress but not the other UPR sensors, including – surprisingly – ATF6β, or SREBP.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: Ceapins prevent selection of ATF6α into COPII vesicles by retaining it in foci in the ER membrane.
source: Using Ceapins to interrogate each step of ATF6α activation, we show here that Ceapins prevent selection of ATF6α into COPII vesicles by retaining it in foci in the ER membrane.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by experimental data.

claim: Removing the requirement for trafficking by bringing together substrate and proteases restored cleavage in the presence of Ceapins.
source: Removing the requirement for trafficking by bringing together substrate and proteases restored cleavage in the presence of Ceapins.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by experimental data.

claim: Ceapins induce rapid clustering of ATF6α.
source: Ceapins induce rapid clustering of ATF6α, indicating that its oligomeric state plays a key role to regulate its trafficking and thereby activation in response to ER stress.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by experimental data.

claim: The oligomeric state of ATF6α plays a key role to regulate its trafficking and thereby activation in response to ER stress.
source: Ceapins induce rapid clustering of ATF6α, indicating that its oligomeric state plays a key role to regulate its trafficking and thereby activation in response to ER stress.
evidence: The statement is an inference drawn from the Ceapin-induced clustering data.

claim: Ceapins are named after the Irish verb 'ceap,' meaning 'to trap'.
source: Based on its mode of action corralling ATF6α into ER-restricted foci, we named Ceapins after the Irish verb 'ceap,' meaning 'to trap' .
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: In unstressed cells, GFP-ATF6α localized to the ER.
source: In unstressed cells, GFP-ATF6α localized to the ER (Figure 1A and E, green).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 1A and E.

claim: After induction of ER stress by treatment with thapsigargin or tunicamycin, a fraction of the GFP fluorescence was observed in the nucleus.
source: As expected, after induction of ER stress by treatment with thapsigargin (Tg), which inhibits the ER calcium pump, or tunicamycin (Tm), which inhibits N-linked glycosylation, we observed a fraction of the GFP fluorescence in the nucleus, apparent by co-localization with DAPI-stained nuclear DNA (Figure 1B and F, DNA in purple, co-localization indicated by white color in overlay).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 1B and F.

claim: Induction of ER stress in the presence of active Ceapin-A7 prevented nuclear translocation of GFP-ATF6α-N and led to an accumulation of GFP fluorescence in discrete foci.
source: Induction of ER stress in the presence of active Ceapin-A7 (Figure 1C and G) but not of the inactive Ceapin analog A5 (Figure 1D and H) prevented nuclear translocation of GFP-ATF6α-N and led to an accumulation of GFP fluorescence in discrete foci (quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 1C and G.

claim: The inactive Ceapin analog A5 did not prevent nuclear translocation of GFP-ATF6α-N.
source: Induction of ER stress in the presence of active Ceapin-A7 (Figure 1C and G) but not of the inactive Ceapin analog A5 (Figure 1D and H) prevented nuclear translocation of GFP-ATF6α-N and led to an accumulation of GFP fluorescence in discrete foci (quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 1D and H.

claim: Under conditions where active Ceapin analogs block ATF6α proteolysis, the foci correspond to a pool of uncleaved GFP-ATF6α.
source: We have previously shown [accompanying manuscript; Gallagher et al., 2016] that under these conditions active Ceapin analogs block ATF6α proteolysis, indicating that the foci correspond to a pool of uncleaved GFP-ATF6α.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by a reference to the accompanying manuscript.

claim: Addition of active Ceapin analogs (Ceapin-A1 and Ceapin-A7) induces formation of GFP-ATF6α foci.
source: The addition of Ceapin analogs induces formation of GFP-ATF6α foci and either partially (K, Ceapin-A1) or completely (L, Ceapin-A7) inhibits nuclear translocation of GFP-ATF6α in response to ER stress.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 1K and L.

claim: Active Ceapin analogs induce GFP-ATF6α foci even in the absence of ER stress.
source: Importantly, we observed that active but not inactive Ceapin analogs induce GFP-ATF6α foci even in the absence of ER stress (Figure 1M and N, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and these foci persist for up to twenty-four hours (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 1M and N.

claim: Ceapin-induced GFP-ATF6α foci persist for up to twenty-four hours.
source: Importantly, we observed that active but not inactive Ceapin analogs induce GFP-ATF6α foci even in the absence of ER stress (Figure 1M and N, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and these foci persist for up to twenty-four hours (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Foci are observed in cells subjected to ER stress alone at later time points corresponding to the time point at which attenuation of ATF6α signaling would initiate.
source: Interestingly we also see foci in cells subjected to ER stress alone at later time points corresponding to the time point at which attenuation of ATF6α signaling would initiate (Figure 1J, 90 min time point and Video 2) (Haze et al., 2001; Rutkowski et al., 2006).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 1J and citations (Haze et al., 2001; Rutkowski et al., 2006).

claim: Washout of both Ceapin-A1 and Ceapin-A7 led to rapid dissolution of GFP-ATF6α foci.
source: We allowed foci to form for 17 min, then washed the cells, and added media without inhibitors. Washout of both Ceapin analogs led to rapid dissolution of GFP-ATF6α foci, indicating the foci formation was reversible (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 2B and C.

claim: Ceapin-induced foci formation is reversible.
source: Washout of both Ceapin analogs led to rapid dissolution of GFP-ATF6α foci, indicating the foci formation was reversible (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 2B and C.

claim: The same molecules of GFP-ATF6α clustered into foci by Ceapins are redistributed in the ER upon washout.
source: We observed the same washout kinetics in cells pretreated for three hours with cycloheximide to inhibit protein synthesis, a time point at which it is reasonable to expect any newly translated GFP-ATF6α had folded and matured (Heim et al., 1994; 1995; Cormack et al., 1996; Li et al., 1998; Sacchetti, 2001; Sacchetti et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2006; Pédelacq et al., 2006; Ugrinov and Clark, 2010) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Videos 10–13). This result indicates that the same molecules of GFP-ATF6α clustered into foci by Ceapins are redistributed in the ER upon washout.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations.

claim: After washout of Ceapins, both control and Ceapin-treated cells responded to ER stress with the same kinetics, showing nuclear accumulation of GFP-ATF6α-N.
source: After the washout, both control and Ceapin-treated cells responded to ER stress with the same kinetics, showing nuclear accumulation of GFP-ATF6α-N (Figure 2E and G, 85 min time point).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 2E and G.

claim: The dissolution of GFP-ATF6α foci restores an activatable pool of GFP-ATF6α.
source: These results suggest that the dissolution of GFP-ATF6α foci restores an activatable pool of GFP-ATF6α.
evidence: The statement is an inference drawn from the washout and re-activation data.

claim: Ceapins are reversible inhibitors of ATF6α.
source: Thus, Ceapins are reversible inhibitors of ATF6α.
evidence: The statement is an inference drawn from the washout experiments.

claim: In the absence of ER stress, there is little overlap between GFP-ATF6α and giantin.
source: In the absence of ER stress, we observed little overlap between GFP-ATF6α and giantin (Figure 3A; giantin staining in purple, see arrowheads in zoomed view).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 3A.

claim: In the presence of ER stress, there is clear co-localization of GFP-ATF6α and giantin.
source: In contrast, in the presence of ER stress, we observed clear co-localization of GFP-ATF6α and giantin (Figure 3B).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Golgi apparatus localization of GFP-ATF6α is markedly enhanced upon treatment of ER stressed cells with S1P inhibitor.
source: Golgi apparatus localization was markedly enhanced upon treatment of ER stressed cells with S1P inhibitor, which blocks the Golgi-resident protease that initiates ATF6α processing (Figure 3C).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: Under S1P inhibitor treatment conditions, GFP-ATF6α traffics to the Golgi apparatus, where it accumulates because it cannot be cleaved.
source: This result was expected as under these conditions GFP-ATF6α traffics to the Golgi apparatus, where it accumulates because it cannot be cleaved (Okada et al., 2003).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by a citation (Okada et al., 2003).

claim: GFP-ATF6α foci formed in the presence of Ceapin-A1 and ER stress did not co-localize with giantin.
source: In contrast, GFP-ATF6α foci formed in the presence of Ceapin-A1 and ER stress did not co-localize with giantin (Figure 3D).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 3D.

claim: ATF6α is not cleaved in the presence of active Ceapin analogs because it does not traffic to the Golgi apparatus upon induction of ER stress.
source: This result suggests that ATF6α is not cleaved in the presence of active Ceapin analogs because it does not traffic to the Golgi apparatus upon induction of ER stress.
evidence: The statement is an inference drawn from the lack of co-localization with Golgi markers.

claim: In unstressed cells, 3xFLAG-ATF6α is found in the ER, co-localizing with the ER marker calnexin.
source: In unstressed cells, we found 3xFLAG-ATF6α in the ER, co-localizing with the ER marker calnexin (Figure 3E).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 3E.

claim: Thirty minutes after induction of ER stress, a portion of 3xFLAG-ATF6α had moved out of the ER.
source: Thirty minutes after induction of ER stress, a portion of 3xFLAG-ATF6α had moved out of the ER (Figure 3F, arrowheads in zoomed views).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 3F.

claim: Treatment of cells with Ceapin-A1, either in the presence or absence of ER stress, led to formation of 3xFLAG-ATF6α foci that decorated ER tubules.
source: Treatment of these cells with Ceapin-A1, either in the presence (Figure 3G) or absence (Figure 3H) of ER stress, led to formation of 3xFLAG-ATF6α foci that decorated ER tubules (arrowheads in zoomed views).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 3G and H.

claim: ER stress induced co-localization of 3xFLAG-ATF6α with giantin.
source: As expected, ER stress induced co-localization of 3xFLAG-ATF6α with giantin (Figure 3J).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 3J.

claim: No co-localization of 3xFLAG-ATF6α with giantin was observed upon co-treatment with Ceapin-A1.
source: No such co-localization was observed upon co-treatment with Ceapin-A1 (Figure 3K).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 3K.

claim: The Ceapin-induced formation of ATF6α foci is independent of the nature of the tag and likely reflects an intrinsic property of ATF6α.
source: Thus the Ceapin-induced formation of ATF6α foci is independent of the nature of the tag and likely reflects an intrinsic property of ATF6α.
evidence: The statement is an inference drawn from the observation that both GFP-ATF6α and 3xFLAG-ATF6α form foci.

claim: After 2.4 hr of ER stress, GFP-ATF6α showed pronounced Golgi apparatus localization with some ER staining remaining.
source: After 2.4 hr of ER stress, GFP-ATF6α showed pronounced Golgi apparatus localization with some ER staining remaining (Figure 3N).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 3N.

claim: In the presence of active Ceapin analogs after 2.4 hr, GFP-ATF6α foci decorated ER tubules and show minimal co-localization with the Golgi marker.
source: In the presence of active Ceapin analogs, GFP-ATF6α foci decorated ER tubules and show minimal co-localization with the Golgi marker (Figure 3O and P).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 3O and P.

claim: In different cell types and using different ATF6α variants, Ceapins induce ATF6α foci and prevent ATF6α trafficking to the Golgi apparatus in response to ER stress.
source: Taken together, these results show that in different cell types and using different ATF6α variants, Ceapins induce ATF6α foci and prevent ATF6α trafficking to the Golgi apparatus in response to ER stress.
evidence: The statement is an inference drawn from the data across different cell types and ATF6α variants.

claim: Endogenous ATF6α is not evenly distributed but found in small foci that are finely distributed over the ER network in unstressed cells.
source: To our surprise, we found that, even in unstressed cells, endogenous ATF6α was not evenly distributed but found in small foci that were finely distributed over the ER network (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 4A–D.

claim: After two hours of ER stress, a portion of endogenous ATF6α co-localized with the Golgi marker GM130.
source: After two hours of ER stress, a portion of endogenous ATF6α co-localized with the Golgi marker GM130 (Figure 4B", arrowheads in inserts), and we observed a significant portion of ATF6α staining in the nucleus (Figure 4B and B', quantified in Figure 4E, bar 2, p<0.0001).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 4B".

claim: After two hours of ER stress, a significant portion of endogenous ATF6α staining was observed in the nucleus.
source: After two hours of ER stress, a portion of endogenous ATF6α co-localized with the Golgi marker GM130 (Figure 4B", arrowheads in inserts), and we observed a significant portion of ATF6α staining in the nucleus (Figure 4B and B', quantified in Figure 4E, bar 2, p<0.0001).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 4B and B'.

claim: Ceapin-A7 reduced co-localization of endogenous ATF6α with GM130.
source: Ceapin-A7 reduced co-localization of ATF6α with GM130 (GM130, Figure 4C", arrowheads in inserts) and blocked nuclear accumulation of ATF6α, retaining it in ER foci (Figure 4C', quantified in Figure 4E, bar 3, p<0.0001).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 4C".

claim: Ceapin-A7 blocked nuclear accumulation of endogenous ATF6α, retaining it in ER foci.
source: Ceapin-A7 reduced co-localization of ATF6α with GM130 (GM130, Figure 4C", arrowheads in inserts) and blocked nuclear accumulation of ATF6α, retaining it in ER foci (Figure 4C', quantified in Figure 4E, bar 3, p<0.0001).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 4C'.

claim: After two hours of treatment with Ceapin-A7 in the absence or presence of ER stress, endogenous ATF6α foci appeared larger and brighter than in unstressed cells.
source: After two hours of treatment with Ceapin-A7 in the absence or presence of ER stress, ATF6α foci appeared larger and brighter than in unstressed cells (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 4C and D.

claim: Endogenous ATF6α largely phenocopies the behavior of its tagged-variants.
source: The data show that endogenous ATF6α largely phenocopies the behavior of its tagged-variants characterized above and reveal that at physiological expression levels and in the absence of ER stress ATF6α is already clustered in small foci in the ER membrane.
evidence: The statement is an inference drawn from the comparison of endogenous and tagged ATF6α behavior.

claim: At physiological expression levels and in the absence of ER stress, ATF6α is already clustered in small foci in the ER membrane.
source: The data show that endogenous ATF6α largely phenocopies the behavior of its tagged-variants characterized above and reveal that at physiological expression levels and in the absence of ER stress ATF6α is already clustered in small foci in the ER membrane.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by data on endogenous ATF6α.

claim: Ceapins may further stabilize ATF6α foci, trapping ATF6α in the ER and thus preventing its Golgi apparatus trafficking and nuclear translocation.
source: Ceapins may further stabilize these foci, trapping ATF6α in the ER and thus preventing its Golgi apparatus trafficking and nuclear translocation.
evidence: The statement is speculative, suggesting a mechanism for Ceapin action.

claim: Brefeldin A treatment fuses the Golgi apparatus and ER compartments and thus relocalizes both S1P and S2P proteases to the ER where they process ATF6α.
source: Brefeldin A treatment fuses the Golgi apparatus and ER compartments (Fujiwara et al., 1988) and thus relocalizes both S1P and S2P proteases to the ER where they process ATF6α (Shen and Prywes, 2004).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by citations (Fujiwara et al., 1988; Shen and Prywes, 2004).

claim: ATF6α-N was produced upon treatment of cells with brefeldin A.
source: As expected, ATF6α-N was produced upon treatment of cells with brefeldin A (Figure 5A, lanes 2, 12, 14, 24) or thapsigargin (Figure 5B, lanes 26, 36, 38, 48).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 5A.

claim: Treatment with both S1P inhibitor and either brefeldin A or thapsigargin prevented ATF6α cleavage.
source: Treatment with both S1P inhibitor and either brefeldin A (Figure 5A, lanes 7–10), or thapsigargin (Figure 5B, lanes 31–34), prevented ATF6α cleavage indicating that changing the subcellular localization of the protease had no effect on the efficacy of its inhibitor.
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 5A and B.

claim: Changing the subcellular localization of S1P had no effect on the efficacy of its inhibitor.
source: Treatment with both S1P inhibitor and either brefeldin A (Figure 5A, lanes 7–10), or thapsigargin (Figure 5B, lanes 31–34), prevented ATF6α cleavage indicating that changing the subcellular localization of the protease had no effect on the efficacy of its inhibitor.
evidence: The statement is an inference drawn from the data showing S1P inhibitor works in both ER and Golgi.

claim: Treatment of cells with active Ceapin analogs did not prevent production of ATF6α-N in brefeldin A-treated cells.
source: In contrast, treatment of cells with active Ceapin analogs did not prevent production of ATF6α-N in brefeldin A-treated cells (Figure 5A, lanes 3–6 and lanes 15–18), whereas it did prevent production of ATF6α-N in thapsigargin-treated cells (Figure 5B, lanes 27–30 and lanes 39–42).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 5A.

claim: Treatment of cells with active Ceapin analogs prevented production of ATF6α-N in thapsigargin-treated cells.
source: In contrast, treatment of cells with active Ceapin analogs did not prevent production of ATF6α-N in brefeldin A-treated cells (Figure 5A, lanes 3–6 and lanes 15–18), whereas it did prevent production of ATF6α-N in thapsigargin-treated cells (Figure 5B, lanes 27–30 and lanes 39–42).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 5B.

claim: The inactive Ceapin analog A5 had no effect on ATF6α cleavage in either brefeldin A or thapsigargin treatment.
source: As expected, the inactive Ceapin analog A5 had no effect on either treatment (Figure 5A, lanes 19–22 and Figure 5B, lanes 43–46).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 5A and B.

claim: Ceapins do not convert ATF6α to an inaccessible or uncleavable form.
source: These results show that Ceapins do not convert ATF6α to an inaccessible or uncleavable form.
evidence: The statement is an inference drawn from the brefeldin A experiment showing ATF6α can be cleaved in the presence of Ceapins when proteases are relocated.

claim: Cleavage of ATF6α in response to ER stress is inhibited because ATF6α does not traffic to the compartment where the proteases required for cleavage reside.
source: Instead, cleavage of ATF6α in response to ER stress is inhibited because ATF6α does not traffic to the compartment where the proteases required for cleavage reside.
evidence: The statement is an inference drawn from the brefeldin A experiment.

claim: In unstressed cells, there is minimal overlap of GFP-ATF6α foci and SEC16/SEC31A double-positive foci.
source: In unstressed cells, we observed minimal overlap of GFP-ATF6α foci and SEC16/SEC31A double-positive foci (Figure 6A, quantified in Figure 6F).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 6A and F.

source: In addition, ATF6α signaling attenuates in the face of unmitigated ER stress: although ATF6α is still plentiful in the ER, its proteolytic cleavage to produce ATF6α-N is only observed at early time points after induction of ER stress (Haze et al., 2001; Rutkowski et al., 2006).
evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by citations (Haze et al., 2001; Rutkowski et al., 2006).

evidence: The statement is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by experimental data.

evidence: The statement is a model proposed based on the data and supported by a citation (Nadanaka et al., 2007).

evidence: The statement is a model proposed based on the data.
